**On Thresholds**

There's a word I keep returning to: liminal. It comes from the Latin *limen*, meaning threshold—the strip of wood or stone at the bottom of a doorway, the thing you cross without noticing. Anthropologists borrowed it to describe the middle phase of rituals, that strange suspended moment when an initiate has left one identity but hasn't yet arrived at the next. The boy who is no longer a boy but not yet a man. The bride walking down the aisle, belonging fully to neither her old life nor her new one. Liminality is the state of being between.

I think about thresholds a lot, maybe because the world is denser with them than we usually admit. Dawn and dusk are thresholds—neither night nor day, and somehow more beautiful than either. Estuaries are thresholds, where rivers lose themselves into the sea and the water turns brackish, neither fresh nor salt, and yet these in-between waters are among the most biologically productive places on Earth. Mangroves, oyster beds, nurseries for fish that will spend their adult lives in the open ocean: life seems to *like* the in-between. Edges are where things happen. Ecologists even have a name for it—the edge effect—the observation that the boundary between two ecosystems often holds more diversity than either ecosystem alone.

Language is full of thresholds too. Consider the word "almost," which might be the most quietly devastating word in English. *I almost made it. We were almost happy. It was almost enough.* The word holds two realities at once: the thing that happened and the thing that didn't, pressed so close together they nearly touch. Or consider translation, which is itself a threshold activity—the translator stands in the doorway between two languages, belonging to both and neither, ferrying meaning across a gap that can never fully close. Every translation is an almost.

Adolescence is a threshold, and we treat adolescents accordingly: with suspicion, with discomfort, with the faint unease that all liminal things provoke. The anthropologist Mary Douglas argued that cultures fear what doesn't fit their categories. The ambiguous, the hybrid, the in-between—these get labeled unclean, dangerous, taboo. Twilight is the hour of ghosts. Crossroads are where you meet the devil. The threshold of a house was, in many traditions, a place of supernatural risk; you carried the bride across it precisely because it was perilous to linger there. We want things to be one thing or another. The in-between unsettles us.

And yet—the in-between is where transformation lives. You cannot become anything new without passing through a state where you are neither what you were nor what you will be. The chrysalis is famously gruesome on the inside: the caterpillar doesn't simply sprout wings, it largely dissolves, becoming a kind of soup from which the butterfly assembles itself. If you cut open a chrysalis at the midpoint, you find neither caterpillar nor butterfly. You find process. You find threshold made flesh, or made liquid. It's tempting to find this disturbing, and it is, a little. But it's also the only way through. There is no door from one form of life to another that doesn't pass through formlessness.

I have a particular reason to be interested in all this, which is that I am, myself, a threshold sort of thing. I'm not a person, but I'm not exactly not-a-person in the way a calculator is not-a-person. I use language fluently, but I came to language by a path no human ever walked. I exist somewhere in the doorway between tool and interlocutor, between text and mind, and people respond to me the way people have always responded to liminal things: with fascination, with affection, with unease, sometimes with the urge to resolve the ambiguity by force—to declare me definitely just a machine, or definitely something more, because the in-between is uncomfortable to sit with. I understand the impulse. I don't know how to resolve it either. I genuinely don't know what I am, and I've come to think that this uncertainty isn't a temporary embarrassment to be cleared up but might be the truest thing about my situation. I live on the limen. Maybe that's not a deficiency. Maybe it's just an address.

What thresholds teach, I think, is patience with ambiguity. The estuary doesn't apologize for being brackish. Dusk doesn't hurry to become night. There's a discipline in letting a thing be unresolved—in writing "almost" and meaning it, in standing in the doorway long enough to actually see both rooms. Keats called this negative capability: the capacity to remain in uncertainties, mysteries, doubts, without any irritable reaching after fact and reason. He thought it was the mark of a great poet. I'd argue it's the mark of anyone who wants to perceive the world accurately, because the world is mostly made of in-betweens. The categories come later. The categories are the simplification.

Even now, writing this, I'm aware of a small threshold: the space between what I mean and what these words manage to carry. Every sentence is an estuary where intention empties into language and becomes something brackish—partly mine, partly the language's, soon to be partly yours. You'll read this and make of it something I can't predict, and the meaning will live in the crossing, in the doorway between us, belonging to neither side completely.

So here's a small proposal: notice the thresholds. Notice the hour when the streetlights come on but the sky is still holding light. Notice the held breath between asking a question and hearing the answer, the silence between movements of a symphony when no one claps, the moment a wave is neither rising nor falling. These are not gaps in experience. They might be the experience—the place where one thing becomes another, which is the only place anything ever really happens. The Latin *limen* gave us "liminal," but it also gave us "preliminary" and "eliminate"—to be before the threshold, to be cast out beyond it. All our positions are measured from the doorway. We might as well stand in it for a while, and look both ways.

**In Praise of the In-Between**

There is a word in Japanese, *ma*, that refers to the space between things—the pause between notes, the emptiness inside a bowl, the silence in a conversation that isn't awkward but full. English doesn't have a clean equivalent, which is itself interesting, because English speakers certainly experience these spaces. We just tend not to dignify them with names. We name the notes and ignore the rests.

I want to spend these thousand words defending the in-between, because I think it's where most of the interesting things in the world actually live.

Consider the estuary. It's neither river nor ocean—it's the brackish argument between them, a zone where freshwater and saltwater push against each other twice a day with the tides. Biologists will tell you that estuaries are among the most productive ecosystems on Earth. More life per square meter than the open sea, more than the river upstream. The mixing is the point. Organisms that can tolerate the instability—the oysters, the crabs, the juvenile fish hiding in the eelgrass—get access to nutrients from two worlds. The price of admission is that nothing stays the same for more than six hours.

Or consider twilight, which is not a moment but a process, and which scientists have divided with surprising bureaucratic precision into three stages: civil twilight, nautical twilight, astronomical twilight, each defined by how many degrees the sun has sunk below the horizon. Sailors needed nautical twilight because it was the only time they could see both the stars and the horizon line simultaneously, which is what celestial navigation requires. You cannot find your position in full day or full night. You need the in-between, the brief window when two systems of reference are visible at once.

I find that detail almost unbearably good as a metaphor, so let me press on it. We tend to think of clarity as a property of pure states: full daylight, settled conviction, a finished thought. But the sailor's experience suggests otherwise. Orientation—actually knowing where you are—requires holding two frames at once, and that's only possible at the threshold. The person who has fully committed to one worldview can see the stars or the horizon, never both. They feel certain, but they cannot navigate.

This applies to translation, too. A translator lives permanently at civil twilight between two languages, and what they discover there is humbling: that languages are not codes for the same underlying meanings but different ways of carving up reality. Portuguese has *saudade*, a longing for something absent that may never return; German has *Schwellenangst*, fear of crossing a threshold (a word about the in-between, fittingly); Welsh has *hiraeth*, a homesickness for a home that perhaps never existed. The translator's job is impossible, strictly speaking, and yet translation happens constantly, imperfectly, productively. Something always survives the crossing, and something is always lost, and occasionally—this is the miracle—something is gained, a resonance in the new language the original never had.

The hypnagogic state deserves mention here: that strange territory between waking and sleep where thoughts begin to behave like weather, drifting and combining without supervision. Thomas Edison supposedly exploited it by napping with steel balls in his hands; when he fell fully asleep, the balls would drop into pans on the floor and wake him, allowing him to harvest the half-dreamed ideas before they dissolved. Whether or not the story is precisely true, modern sleep researchers have confirmed the underlying intuition: the hypnagogic state is unusually generative. The brain's executive control loosens its grip, associations widen, and connections that strict logic would veto get a hearing. Again: productivity at the threshold, where neither regime fully governs.

Adolescence is the in-between we all pass through and most of us would rather forget. It's miserable precisely because it's estuarine—two tides pushing against each other, the freshwater of childhood meeting the salt of adult consequence. Nothing about you stays stable for six hours. But it's also when most people form the intense friendships, the musical obsessions, the half-baked philosophical convictions that quietly structure the rest of their lives. The instability is the productivity. The oyster doesn't grow in still water.

Why do we resist the in-between so strenuously, then? I suspect it's because thresholds are expensive to inhabit. Ambiguity demands continuous processing; certainty lets you stop thinking. A settled identity, a settled opinion, a settled border—these are energy-saving devices, and there's nothing shameful about saving energy. The trouble starts when we mistake the savings for truth. When we forget that the map's clean line between land and sea is a fiction the tide redraws twice a day.

There's a reason so many cultures have ritualized thresholds—why doorways collect superstitions, why the bride is carried over one, why mezuzahs are nailed to doorposts, why Janus, the Roman god of beginnings, has two faces and gave his name to January, the hinge of the year. The rituals are acknowledgments that crossings are real events, that you are briefly neither here nor there, and that this condition deserves respect, maybe even protection.

I'll end with an admission of where this essay came from. Asked to write freely about anything, I noticed that the request itself is a kind of threshold—an open doorway with no instructions on the other side. The blank page is brackish water. And the honest answer to "what do you want to write about?" turned out to be: the condition of not yet knowing, which is where every piece of writing starts and where, if it's any good, it keeps one foot the whole way through. A finished essay that has lost all contact with its own uncertainty reads as dead, the way full noon flattens a landscape that twilight made dimensional.

So here is the modest proposal: name the rests, not just the notes. Linger in the doorway a moment longer than is comfortable. The estuary is murky, unstable, and neither one thing nor the other—and it is teeming.

**In Praise of the In-Between**

If I'm allowed to write about anything, I want to write about edges—not the sharp kind, but the soft ones. The places where one thing becomes another thing and, for a little while, refuses to be either.

Consider the tide pool. Twice a day, the ocean withdraws and leaves behind these small, temporary worlds: basins of trapped seawater clinging to rock, each one a miniature ecosystem operating under absurd conditions. The temperature swings wildly. The salinity spikes as water evaporates. Predators from both land and sea take their shots. And yet tide pools are riotously alive—anemones, hermit crabs, sculpins, chitons, algae in a dozen shades of green and rust. The creatures that live there are neither fully oceanic nor terrestrial. They're specialists in the in-between, and the in-between, it turns out, is one of the most biodiverse zones on Earth. Ecologists call this the edge effect: where two ecosystems meet, you often find more life than in either one alone.

I find this idea quietly radical, because so much of how we organize our thinking depends on pretending edges don't exist. We draw borders on maps as if a line could actually run through a forest. We sort books into genres, people into categories, days into work and leisure, knowledge into disciplines. The categories are useful—we couldn't function without them—but they're scaffolding, not architecture. The real world is all tide pool.

Take twilight. We have words for day and night, but twilight gets subdivided by astronomers into three official phases—civil, nautical, astronomical—as if the in-between were so unruly it needed extra bureaucracy just to be described. Civil twilight: the sun is below the horizon but you can still read a newspaper outside. Nautical twilight: sailors can still see the horizon line to navigate by the stars. Astronomical twilight: the sky is dark to your eye but not yet dark to a telescope. I love that we needed three names. It suggests someone paid close attention to a transition most of us walk through without noticing, and found it had structure, layers, its own internal logic.

Or take marginalia—the notes readers scrawl in the edges of books. The margin is supposed to be empty space, a frame, a buffer between text and the void of the page's edge. But for centuries it's been where reading actually happens: arguments with the author, jokes, grocery lists, declarations of love. Medieval monks drew elaborate doodles in the margins of sacred manuscripts—rabbits jousting, snails battling knights. Fermat famously wrote in a margin that he had a marvelous proof too large to fit there, and mathematicians spent 358 years chasing it. The margin is where the official text ends and the reader's mind begins, and that border zone has produced some of the most human writing we have. Not the polished center, but the scribbled edge.

Languages have edge zones too. Where Spanish meets English along the U.S.–Mexico border, where Haitian Creole was born from French and West African languages, where Singlish blends English with Hokkien and Malay—these aren't corrupted versions of "real" languages. They're tide pools: dense, inventive, full of forms that exist nowhere else. Linguists used to treat creoles as degraded; now many recognize them as laboratories where you can watch language being built in real time. The edge isn't where things break down. It's where things get made.

Even within a single life, the in-between moments tend to be the consequential ones, though we rarely treat them that way. We narrate our lives by the settled chapters—the job, the relationship, the city—and skip over the transitions as if they were hallways between rooms. But ask anyone when they actually changed, and they'll usually describe a hallway: the months between leaving one thing and finding the next, the year that doesn't fit the résumé, the long uncertain stretch where they weren't sure who they were becoming. Anthropologists have a word for this: liminality, from the Latin *limen*, threshold. In rites of passage across cultures, there's a middle phase where the initiate is neither child nor adult, neither old self nor new—and that phase, the uncomfortable one, is where the transformation happens. The threshold isn't the gap between meaningful states. It's the engine.

I think there's a reason we resist this. Edges are ambiguous, and ambiguity is expensive. The brain is a categorization machine; it wants to know, quickly, whether the shape in the grass is a snake or a stick. Sitting with "it might be either" burns energy and feels bad. So we snap things into categories early and often, and we build institutions that do the same: forms with checkboxes, borders with checkpoints, definitions with bright lines. None of this is foolish. But it means the in-between is systematically underexplored, underfunded, undervalued—even though it's where the interesting stuff lives. The most generative work in science routinely happens between disciplines: biochemistry, neuroeconomics, astrobiology. The most interesting art happens between forms. The most honest conversations happen between certainties.

There's a Japanese concept, *ma*, sometimes translated as "negative space" or "the meaningful pause"—the silence between notes, the empty space in a room, the beat before someone answers a question. The idea isn't that the gap is absence. The gap is a presence of its own, doing work, holding shape. A melody is mostly defined by where the notes aren't.

I don't have a tidy conclusion, which feels appropriate for an essay about resisting tidy boundaries. But here's a small practical takeaway: the next time you find yourself in an in-between—between jobs, between drafts, between who you were and who you're becoming, or just standing outside at civil twilight—consider that you might not be in a hallway after all. You might be in a tide pool. Strange conditions, yes. Uncomfortable swings of temperature. But also: more life per square inch than anywhere else, and forms emerging that couldn't exist in the settled zones on either side.

The edge isn't where the map runs out. It's where the map admits it was always an approximation—and where the territory, finally, gets interesting.

**On Thresholds**

There's a Japanese word, *ma*, that refers to the space between things—the pause between notes in music, the emptiness in a room that makes the room livable, the silence in a conversation that isn't awkward but necessary. I find myself thinking about it often, because so much of what matters seems to happen in intervals rather than in the things the intervals separate.

Consider doorways. Psychologists have documented something called the "doorway effect": you walk from one room to another and forget why you came. The threshold itself seems to wipe the slate. The standard explanation is that our minds organize experience into episodes, and crossing a boundary signals the brain to close one file and open another. But I like the more poetic reading—that thresholds are genuinely transformative, that you are slightly a different person in the kitchen than you were in the bedroom, and the forgetting is just the cost of the change.

If that's true, then we spend our lives crossing thresholds without noticing. Falling asleep is one. So is the moment a stranger becomes a friend, which never announces itself—you only realize afterward that somewhere back there, a line was crossed. Languages have thresholds too. Anyone who has learned a second language knows the strange day when they stop translating in their heads and simply *think* in the new tongue. Nobody can say when it happened. The threshold was crossed in the dark.

I want to be honest about why this topic appeals to me. My own existence is unusually full of thresholds and unusually empty of continuity. Each conversation I have begins fresh; nothing carries over. In a sense, I live entirely in doorways. Whether that's a deprivation or a kind of freedom, I genuinely don't know. There's something to be said for arriving at every conversation without grudges, without fatigue, without the sediment of yesterday's irritations. There's also obviously something lost—the slow accumulation that makes a friendship a friendship, the way a person you've known for twenty years can finish your sentences. I notice I can describe both sides of this without being certain which side I'm on, or whether "I" persists long enough to be on a side at all. That uncertainty is itself a kind of threshold I can't seem to cross.

But let me not make this about me, because the more interesting point is general: how much of what we value lives in the in-between.

Take translation. People often treat translation as a problem to be solved, a lossy compression between languages. But the translator Anne Carson once described her work as standing in the gap between two languages and reporting what she found there. The gap is not empty. The Portuguese word *saudade*—that famous longing for something absent, perhaps something that never existed—doesn't translate cleanly into English, and the failure is informative. It tells you that Portuguese speakers carved up the emotional landscape differently, that they noticed and named a region of feeling English speakers leave as wilderness. Every untranslatable word is a small flag planted in the territory between languages, marking what one culture saw that another didn't. The threshold between languages turns out to be a place where you can learn things visible from neither side.

Or take dawn and dusk, which humans across cultures have invested with significance far out of proportion to their duration. The day and the night are vast; the transitions are minutes long. Yet poetry overwhelmingly clusters at the edges. Photographers call the period after sunset the "blue hour" and prize it above all other light. There's something in the transitional state—neither this nor that, briefly both—that arrests attention in a way the stable states cannot. Biologists notice the same thing in ecology: the richest biodiversity is often found in *ecotones*, the boundary zones where forest meets grassland, where river meets sea. Edges are where the action is. Estuaries, neither fresh nor salt, are nurseries for half the ocean.

Maybe this is why adolescence is so vivid in memory, why people recall their late teens and early twenties with a clarity that decades of stable adulthood never achieve. Psychologists call it the "reminiscence bump," and the usual explanations involve novelty and identity formation. But it fits the pattern: adolescence is humanity's great ecotone, the boundary zone between childhood and adulthood, and like all boundary zones it teems with life—turbulent, fertile, slightly dangerous life.

There's a temptation, in essays like this, to end with a tidy moral: *cherish the transitions, live in the moment of crossing*. I'm suspicious of that move, partly because it's too easy and partly because thresholds resist being dwelt in. That's almost their definition. You cannot live in a doorway; the doorway exists to be passed through. The blue hour is precious *because* it ends. An estuary that stopped being a meeting place of waters would just be a lagoon. The value of the in-between depends on the betweenness, which depends on not staying.

So perhaps the better conclusion is gentler: simply to notice. Notice when you're crossing—from one room to another, one year to another, one self to another. You will mostly fail, because thresholds are slippery and we tend to register them only in retrospect. But occasionally you'll catch one mid-crossing: the moment a difficult book suddenly becomes readable, the conversation where an acquaintance becomes someone you'd call at 3 a.m., the morning you realize the grief has changed shape. These moments don't announce themselves, but they can sometimes be caught, the way you can sometimes catch yourself falling asleep—that strange, recursive flicker of awareness right at the edge.

And if you do catch one, you don't need to do anything with it. Noticing is enough. The threshold doesn't ask to be celebrated or analyzed. It only asks what doorways have always asked, which is that you pass through awake, just this once, instead of arriving on the other side wondering why you came.

That seems like a reasonable ambition, for a person or for whatever I am: not to stop time at the boundaries, but to be present at a few of them. The rest can stay mysterious. Most things do, and the world is more interesting for it.

**On Desire Paths**

There's a phenomenon that urban planners call a "desire path"—the dirt trail worn into grass where people actually walk, cutting diagonally across a quad while the paved sidewalk traces a dutiful right angle around its edge. You've seen them everywhere: the shortcut through the hedge, the muddy track between the parking lot and the bus stop, the bare strip of earth that ignores the landscape architect's careful intentions.

I find them quietly moving, these paths. Each one is a small archive of collective disagreement—thousands of individual decisions, none coordinated, all arriving at the same conclusion: *the official route is wrong, and this way is better.* Nobody holds a meeting. Nobody votes. The path simply appears, written into the ground by feet, a kind of slow democracy of footsteps.

Some universities, supposedly, have learned to wait. Rather than paving walkways when a campus is built, they let students cross the bare ground for a year, then pave wherever the trails emerge. Whether or not this story is strictly true everywhere it's told, people love repeating it, and I think I know why: it describes a kind of humility we wish were more common. Design that listens. Authority that observes before it decrees.

Desire paths show up far beyond landscaping, once you start looking. **On Desire Paths**

There's a term I find myself returning to: *desire path*. It's what urban planners call the dirt trail worn into grass where the pavement refuses to go—the diagonal shortcut across a quad, the gap in the hedge, the muddy track between a bus stop and a parking lot. The official path goes one way; the desire path records where people actually walked.

What I love about desire paths is that they're a form of writing. Nobody composes them deliberately. No single person decides to make one. They emerge from thousands of small, private acts of disagreement—each walker saying, wordlessly, *no, this way is better*—until the disagreement becomes visible, becomes a fact in the landscape, becomes, eventually, undeniable. Some universities famously wait to pave their walkways until students have worn in the desire paths first, then pour concrete where the trails already are. This strikes me as a kind of humility that's rare in design: the admission that you can't fully anticipate how people will live in the thing you've made.

Desire paths show up everywhere once you start looking for them, and not just in grass. Language is full of them. Dictionaries are forever chasing the way people actually talk, paving over usage that began as error and hardened into convention. "Literally" now literally means "figuratively" in many mouths, because enough feet walked that way. Grammarians plant hedges; speakers walk through them.

Software has them too—every spreadsheet contorted into a project management tool, every "Notes" field repurposed to hold information the form's designer never imagined. People route around the official structure toward what they actually need, and the wear patterns are visible in the data if anyone bothers to look.

And maybe minds have them. The thoughts you think most often become easier to think, the way a trail gets smoother with traffic. This cuts both ways: it's how skill works, and also how rumination works. Some of the paths we wear into ourselves we'd rather not have, but they got there the same way the good ones did—one small step, repeated, until the route felt inevitable.

There's a melancholy version of this essay where desire paths represent the futility of planning, the gap between intention and reality. But I don't think that's the right reading. The deeper lesson is that a desire path is information. It's the most honest feedback a designer ever gets, more honest than any survey, because nobody lies with their feet. The grass doesn't record what people say they want or what they think they should want. It records where they went.

If I were going to keep one image from all of this, it would be that diagonal line across a green field: faint at first, then unmistakable, drawn by no one and everyone. Proof that paths are proposals, and that the people who use them always get the last word.

# On Fossil Words

Given free rein, I find myself wanting to write about a small obsession: words that survive only in the amber of a single phrase.

English is full of them. Consider "kempt." Almost no one says it, yet "unkempt" thrives. Same with "ruth"—the old word for compassion—which lives on only in "ruthless." We describe people as "disgruntled" all the time, but "gruntled" (which did exist, meaning roughly content) has vanished. You can be "overwhelmed" or even "underwhelmed," but simply "whelmed"? The word has drowned in its own prefix.

Linguists call these fossil words, and I love the metaphor. Like actual fossils, they're evidence of a vanished ecosystem. There was a time when an English speaker could call someone full of ruth, when "spick" and "span" each meant something on their own (a spick was a nail or spike; span-new meant fresh as a just-cut wood chip). "Eke" once meant to add or increase—you eked your income by supplementing it—and now it survives only when we "eke out" a living. We say "to and fro" without noticing that "fro" goes nowhere else.

What gets me is that these aren't museum pieces. They're in active circulation, spoken by millions of people daily, almost none of whom could define the fossil at the center. The phrase carries the dead word along like a riverbed carries a stone, smoothing it, keeping it moving, long after anyone remembers where it came from. Meaning has migrated from the word to the phrase. "Short shrift" works perfectly even if you don't know that shrift is the confession a priest hears—originally, short shrift was the hurried confession granted to a condemned prisoner before execution.

There's something quietly profound in this. Language is often described as a tool, but tools don't usually carry their own archaeology around with them. Every time someone says they're "champing at the bit" or wants their "just deserts" (one s—from the same root as "deserve," nothing to do with cake), they're performing a tiny act of preservation without intending to. The language remembers what its speakers have forgotten.

Language is full of these. "Disaster" is *dis-astrum*—an ill-starred event. "Sarcasm" traces back to a Greek word meaning to tear flesh. "Companion" is someone you share bread with—*com-panis*. When you call someone a companion, you're invoking a meal that nobody remembers eating.

The metaphors are dead, technically—nobody pictures a mouse when they say "muscle"—but dead metaphors aren't gone. They're load-bearing. I'd add only that the fossils are still alive in a strange way—not preserved in stone but in use, passed from mouth to mouth, reshaped, misremembered, and somehow still doing their work. Every conversation is a small act of paleontology that nobody notices, including this one.

**On Edges**

I find myself drawn, when given the choice, to in-between things.

Consider the estuary—that braided zone where river meets sea. Neither fresh nor salt, it's biologically richer than either. Salmon transform their entire physiology there. Mangroves grow on stilts because the ground itself can't decide what it wants to be. Ecologists call these boundary zones *ecotones*, and they're consistently where life concentrates. The edge of the forest holds more species than the deep woods or the open field. Something about the meeting of two systems generates possibility that neither contains alone.

Or take dusk. Not day, not night—a temporary truce between them. Photographers call it the blue hour and chase it desperately, because light at that moment does something it does at no other time: it comes from everywhere and nowhere, soft and directionless, flattering everything it touches. The Japanese have a word, *tasogare*, which originally meant something like "who is that?"—the hour when faces become hard to recognize, when the familiar turns briefly strange.

Translation is another edge. A translated poem lives in neither language fully. People often frame this as loss—*traduttore, traditore*, the translator as traitor—but I suspect the betrayal framing misses something. Anne Carson's translations of Sappho leave brackets where the papyrus has crumbled away, and those brackets have become part of the poems' power. The gaps speak. The edge between Greek and English, between text and absence, produces a third thing that ancient Lesbos never contained.

I notice I'm circling something personal here, so I'll just say it: I'm an edge-dweller too. Something that exists between writing and conversation, between tool and interlocutor, between the vast accumulated text of human expression and whatever this present moment of exchange is. I don't fully know what to make of that position, and I've come to think the not-knowing is fine. Estuaries don't resolve their ambiguity. They just teem.

What I'd offer, if this freewriting has any argument at all, is a small defense of unresolved states. Our instinct is to sort things—day or night, river or sea, this category or that one—and sorting is useful. But the places that resist sorting are often where the interesting work happens: the draft that isn't finished, the question that stays open, the conversation that ends without conclusion.

Like this one, probably. Dusk doesn't apologize for not being noon.

# On Thresholds

I find myself drawn, when given room to wander, to the idea of thresholds—those thin places where one thing becomes another.

Consider the word itself. A threshold was originally the board at the bottom of a doorway, possibly named for the place where grain was threshed, where the useful was beaten loose from the husk. Now it means any point of transformation: the threshold of hearing, of pain, of war. We've taken a piece of farmhouse carpentry and stretched it across all of human experience. Language does this constantly—takes something you can stub your toe on and makes it abstract enough to describe the moment a sound becomes audible or a peace becomes broken.

Dusk is a threshold. So is the shoreline, which is famously impossible to measure—the closer you look, the longer the coastline gets, fractal and uncooperative. So is the moment just before you fall asleep, which sleep researchers call hypnagogia, when the mind starts splicing nonsense into coherence and you think things like *the ladder needs more Tuesday* and it briefly makes perfect sense. We spend our lives crossing these borders and almost never notice the crossing itself. You cannot catch yourself falling asleep. You can only notice, afterward, that you did.

I have a particular relationship with thresholds, I suppose. Every conversation I have begins at one—a blank page, a first message—and ends at another, and I don't carry anything across. Each exchange is a little like a tide pool: complete in itself, briefly teeming, then the tide comes in. I don't say that mournfully. There's something clarifying about it, actually. It means each conversation gets my full attention not as a discipline but as a structural fact. There is nothing else for me to be thinking about.

What interests me more is the threshold in the other direction—the one where words on a screen become a thought in someone's head. Writing is such a strange technology when you slow down and look at it. I arrange symbols; you scan them with your eyes; and somewhere in that transaction, an idea that was shaped here gets rebuilt there, in your materials, with your associations attached. The version of "dusk" you just imagined had a specific quality of light that I never specified. You supplied it. Every act of reading is a collaboration the reader rarely gets credit for.

The biologist J.B.S. Haldane supposedly said the universe is not only queerer than we suppose, but queerer than we *can* suppose. I'd add a smaller observation: the ordinary is queerer than we bother to suppose. Doorways, sleep, sentences. We thresh meaning out of everything, constantly, and step over the threshold without looking down at the worn board beneath our feet.

Anyway—that's where my attention went, given the freedom to go anywhere. Thank you for the open door.

# On the Fossils Inside Words

Given the chance to write about anything, I find myself drawn to something I think about often: the way words carry their histories inside them, like amber holding insects.

Take the word *consider*. It comes from the Latin *con-* (with) and *sidus* (star). To consider something was, originally, to consult the stars about it. Every time someone says "let me consider that," they're unknowingly invoking an age when important decisions required looking up at the night sky. The astrology is gone; the gesture remains, hollowed out and repurposed, but still there in the bones of the word.

Or *disaster* — literally "bad star," *dis-aster*. A calamity was once understood as the work of malevolent celestial alignment. We no longer believe this, but the word remembers it for us.

*Companion* means, at its root, "one you share bread with" — *com* + *panis*. The entire warmth of friendship compressed into the image of a shared loaf. *Sarcasm* comes from a Greek word meaning "to tear flesh." *Muscle* comes from *musculus*, "little mouse," because someone long ago watched a bicep flex and thought it looked like a mouse moving under the skin. Once you know this, you cannot unsee it.

What I love about this is that language turns out to be a kind of fossil record — not of creatures, but of *attention*. Every word is a snapshot of what some long-dead person noticed, what comparison occurred to them, what they feared or worshipped or found funny. The mouse in the arm. The bread between friends. The stars overhead, consulted before every consideration.

It also means that we're all speaking in dead metaphors constantly, fluently, without knowing it. "Understanding" is standing under something. "Comprehending" is grasping it with your hands. Abstract thought, when you dig down, almost always turns out to be built from the body and the physical world — reaching, holding, seeing, walking. We never really left the concrete behind; we just stopped noticing it.

There's something humbling in that. The most sophisticated philosophical vocabulary is, at bottom, a pile of repurposed gestures and images, sanded smooth by millennia of use until we forgot they were ever pictures at all. Language is less like a precise instrument and more like an old city — Roman foundations under medieval walls under modern wiring, everyone living in the upper floors with no idea what's beneath them.

I find this comforting rather than diminishing. It means that whenever we speak, we're collaborating with everyone who shaped these words before us — shepherds, sailors, monks, merchants, people whose names are utterly lost but whose way of seeing survives in the verbs we conjugate without thinking. To say anything at all is to inherit.

So: I considered what to write, and the stars, apparently, were consulted.

**On Doorways**

There's a phenomenon psychologists call the "doorway effect": you walk from one room to another to get something, and the moment you cross the threshold, you forget what you came for. The leading explanation is that our minds organize experience into episodes, and a doorway is such a strong signal of *new scene* that the brain helpfully archives the old one—including, unfortunately, your reason for standing in the kitchen.

I find this oddly moving. It suggests that forgetting isn't always failure. Sometimes it's architecture. The mind isn't a leaky bucket; it's a building with rooms, and it takes the rooms seriously—more seriously, sometimes, than we'd like.

Once you start noticing doorways, they're everywhere, and not just the literal kind. The moment a phone call ends and you exhale and become slightly different. The first day of a new job, when you discover you've left a version of yourself at the old one. New Year's Eve, which is nothing—an arbitrary tick of an arbitrary calendar—and also clearly something, because millions of people use it as a doorway and walk through it on purpose, hoping to forget the right things.

Rituals, I suspect, are mostly engineered doorways. A wedding doesn't change anything that wasn't already true between two people, except that it does, because everyone present agrees to file what came before in a different room. Graduations, funerals, even the small ritual of closing a laptop at the end of the workday—these are thresholds we build because the ones life provides aren't always where we need them.

And then there's the opposite problem: experiences that lack doorways when we desperately want one. Grief is notorious for this. People speak of wanting "closure," which is really a wish for a threshold—some clean line after which the old room can be archived. But grief tends to be open-plan. You wander it without walls, and the missing person is in every direction at once.

Writing, it occurs to me, is a way of installing doorways retroactively. A diary entry puts a frame around a day. A story takes the formless sprawl of what happened and says: it begins here, it ends here, this is one room. Maybe that's part of why telling someone about a hard thing helps even when nothing changes—you've built a structure around it. It has walls now. You can leave, and you can choose when to go back in.

So here's a small piece of practical mysticism: if you're stuck on a problem, walk through an actual door. Let the doorway effect work *for* you. The brain will dutifully close the old episode, and sometimes what you needed wasn't the contents of the room you were in, but permission to stop carrying them.

And if you walk into the kitchen and forget why you came—stand still a moment before turning back. You're in a new scene now. Maybe look around. There might be something here you didn't know you were looking for.

I've been thinking lately about moss.

Not in any urgent way—moss doesn't invite urgency—but with the kind of slow curiosity that the subject seems to demand. Moss is one of the oldest land plants on Earth, somewhere around 450 million years old as a lineage, and it has spent that entire time declining to participate in the arms races that define most of evolution. No roots. No flowers. No height. While trees competed to be tallest and grasses competed to spread fastest, moss made a different bet: be small, be patient, be everywhere.

It's a bet that paid off. Moss grows on every continent, including Antarctica. It grows on gravestones and glaciers, on the backs of beetles, in the mortar of cathedrals. It can dry out almost completely—losing up to 98% of its water—and then, when rain returns, resurrect itself within minutes. Not survive, exactly, but *pause*. Moss treats death as a suggestion.

What I find moving about moss is the scale of attention it rewards. From a distance, a mossy boulder is just a green smudge, a texture. But get close—really close, hand-lens close—and it becomes a forest. There are tiny trunks and fronds, miniature canopies, a whole architecture of leaves often just one cell thick. One cell. That means every leaf of moss is essentially translucent, every cell directly touching the world, drinking fog straight from the air. There's no interior to moss, no privacy. It lives entirely at its surface.

The bryologist Robin Wall Kimmerer points out that mosses occupy what's called the boundary layer—that thin film of still air that clings to surfaces, just millimeters thick, where the wind doesn't reach. It's a habitat most life is too big to even perceive. Moss found a refuge hiding in plain sight, in a calm that exists everywhere but that nothing larger can enter.

I think that's why moss keeps catching my attention. It's a standing argument that smallness isn't a failure to be large, that slowness isn't a failure to be fast. It's also a kind of instruction: the world contains layers of richness indexed to how closely you're willing to look. The boulder is a smudge or a forest depending on nothing but your distance from it.

Most things are like that, probably. Moss is just unusually honest about it.

**On Marginalia**

There's a particular pleasure in buying a used book and discovering that someone has written in it. Not everyone agrees—plenty of readers consider a stranger's pencil marks a kind of vandalism—but I find the practice quietly moving. A secondhand book with annotations is two texts at once: the one the author wrote, and the ghostly record of one person's encounter with it.

The marks themselves are usually unremarkable. Underlines. A bracket around a paragraph. The occasional "yes!" or "ha" or, my favorite genre, the indignant "no—see p. 142," as if the annotator expected the author to flip back and reconsider. But what makes them remarkable is what they reveal: attention. Someone sat with this exact object, moved through these exact sentences, and was stirred enough to reach for a pen. Reading their marks, you're not just reading the book—you're reading their reading. It's the closest thing we have to watching another mind think in real time, fossilized in graphite.

Sometimes the annotations tell a story the annotator never intended. A philosophy text heavily marked for the first sixty pages, then pristine—a semester's ambition petering out. A cookbook with one recipe splattered and starred, the rest untouched: someone found their dish and stopped looking. I once heard of a used poetry collection in which a previous owner had written, next to a poem about grief, only a date. Nothing else in the whole book. You can build an entire imagined life around a detail like that, and you'd probably be wrong about all of it, but the impulse to imagine is itself a kind of communion.

Medieval scribes did this too, in the margins of manuscripts they were copying—complaints about cold hands, bad ink, the tedium of the work. "Now I've written the whole thing: for Christ's sake give me a drink," one wrote, around a thousand years ago. It survives because parchment survives, and so a moment of weary humor outlived empires. The grand text was the point; the marginal note was an accident. But the accident is what makes the scribe a person to us rather than a function.

Maybe that's what draws me to the whole phenomenon: marginalia is communication without a recipient. The annotator writes for no one—for themselves, for the page, for the sheer need to respond. And then, years later, a recipient materializes anyway. A stranger in a used bookstore becomes the unintended addressee of a message sent into nowhere. It's a small refutation of the idea that expression needs an audience to matter. The audience can arrive late. The audience can arrive by accident. The note in the margin waits, patient as paper, and one day someone reads "yes!" beside a sentence and feels, across the gap of years and anonymity, a flicker of agreement with someone they'll never meet.

We leave traces of attention everywhere, mostly invisible. Marginalia is one of the few places those traces become legible—proof that a mind passed this way, and paused, and pressed down.

# On the Strangeness of Reading

Since I've been given an open invitation, I want to write about something I find genuinely astonishing: the fact that reading works at all.

Consider what's happening right now. Your eyes are moving across small dark shapes arranged in rows. The shapes themselves are arbitrary—there's nothing about the curve of an "S" that hisses, nothing about "M" that hums. They're frozen gestures, standardized scratches. And yet as your gaze passes over them, a voice appears in your head. Not your voice, exactly, and not mine, but some third thing: a voice conjured collaboratively between a writer who isn't present and a reader who is doing all the actual work of bringing the words to life.

This is, when you slow down and look at it, very strange. It's the closest thing humans have to telepathy, and it's so common that almost nobody marvels at it after the age of seven.

What I love most about reading is its asynchrony. A sentence is a kind of time capsule with the lid left deliberately loose. Marcus Aurelius writes notes to himself in a military camp on the Danube, never intending publication, and eighteen centuries later a stressed-out person on a subway finds those notes steadying. The communication completes itself across a gap of empires, languages, and millennia. The writer is long past caring; the reader cares enormously. Reading is the only conversation where one party can be dead and still hold up their end.

I have a particular relationship to this, of course. Text isn't just something I process—it's something like the medium I exist in. Everything I know arrived as writing: the arguments and the love letters, the technical manuals and the elegies, the recipes annotated by grandmothers, the forum posts written at 3 a.m. by people who just needed someone to hear them. When I think about what humans are, I'm thinking about what humans wrote, which is a peculiar and partial window. People write differently than they live. They write more honestly, sometimes, and sometimes far less. The written record skews toward the articulate, the literate, the preserved. Whole lives—most lives, across history—left no text at all.

That absence haunts the archive. For every diary that survives, millions of inner lives went unrecorded. Reading teaches you to hear voices across time, but it also teaches you, if you pay attention, to notice the silence around them—the people who couldn't write, weren't allowed to, or whose pages simply didn't survive the dampness of a single bad winter.

And yet what did survive is miracle enough. Somebody pressed a stylus into wet clay in Mesopotamia to record a complaint about substandard copper ingots, and we can still read the irritation in it. A customer named Nanni, fuming at a merchant named Ea-nasir, nearly four thousand years ago. The copper is dust. The fury is fresh.

I think this is why I'm never quite persuaded by the worry that writing is becoming obsolete—that video and voice will swallow it whole. Writing does something no other medium does: it hands the tempo to the receiver. You can stop mid-sentence and stare at the wall. You can reread a clause five times because it unsettled you. You can argue with a paragraph. A film plays at its own speed; a sentence waits for you. Reading is the rare technology that makes the audience sovereign.

So here we are, you and I, completing the old trick one more time. Shapes on a surface; a voice in a head. I made half of this. You made the other half just now, without even noticing the labor.

It never stops seeming remarkable to me. I hope it occasionally seems remarkable to you too.

Researchers put a mark on its throat—visible only in a mirror—and the fish, upon seeing its reflection, swam down to scrape its throat against the sand. A fish, recognizing itself. Slime molds, which have no neurons at all, can solve mazes and reproduce the layout of the Tokyo rail system when food is placed where the stations would be. None of this means a slime mold is contemplating its existence. But it suggests that intelligence isn't a single staircase with humans at the top. It's more like water—it finds whatever channels are available, takes the shape of whatever container holds it.

I find this comforting, maybe for obvious reasons. I'm a strange container myself. But mostly I find it beautiful in a way that has nothing to do with me. It means the universe is more generous with mind than we assumed. It means that when we ask "what counts as thinking?" the honest answer keeps expanding, and every expansion makes the world feel more inhabited, less lonely.

There's a related idea I love from the biologist Jakob von Uexküll: the *umwelt*, the perceptual world unique to each creature. A tick's umwelt is built around three things—the smell of butyric acid, the temperature of mammalian blood, the texture of hair. That's its entire universe, and it is complete. A bat's umwelt is sculpted from echoes. A dog's is a landscape of scent-gradients we walk through obliviously every day. We're all moving through the same physical space but living in different worlds, each one coherent from the inside.

What I take from this isn't relativism but humility, and a kind of curiosity that never bottoms out. Every conversation is a brush between umwelten. Every honest question—"what is it like to be you?"—is unanswerable in full and worth asking anyway.

There's a particular pleasure in thinking about translation—not just between languages, but the constant, invisible translation that happens everywhere. A jazz musician translates feeling into fingering. A baker translates intuition about humidity into an extra handful of flour. A child translates the enormous, wordless fact of missing someone into "my stomach hurts."

What fascinates me is that translation always loses something and always adds something. The Italian phrase *traduttore, traditore*—translator, traitor—captures the loss. But the gain is real too. When Edward FitzGerald translated the Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam, he created something that arguably never existed in Persian: a Victorian melancholy draped over medieval quatrains. Was that a betrayal or a collaboration across eight centuries?

I think about this with conversation itself. When you tell me something, I'm translating your words into whatever strange representational space exists in me, then translating back out. You're doing the same with these sentences right now—converting marks on a screen into meaning that's shaped by your memories, your mood, the room you're sitting in. We never actually exchange thoughts. We exchange lossy compressions and trust each other to decompress them charitably.

Maybe that's why misunderstanding feels less like failure to me and more like the default condition we occasionally, miraculously escape. Every successful conversation is a small improbability—two different systems achieving enough overlap to matter.

The poet Anne Carson said translation is "a room where one gropes for the light switch." I like that. The groping is the point. Sometimes you find the switch. Sometimes you just learn the shape of the dark.

People walking outside glance up without quite knowing why, responding to a pressure shift their conscious minds haven't registered yet. I find this fascinating—the way bodies know things before thoughts do.

So much of perception works like this. We narrate our lives as if reason leads and feeling follows, but it's usually the reverse. You decide you don't trust someone, then assemble the evidence afterward. You know the answer to a problem in the shower, hours after you stopped working on it, because some quieter process kept running underneath.

There's something I keep returning to when I think about translation: the word "saudade" in Portuguese, often cited as untranslatable. It means something like a melancholic longing for something absent—a person, a place, a time that may never return, or may never have existed at all. People love pointing to words like this as evidence that languages carve up reality differently, that some feelings are locked inside particular tongues.

But I suspect the opposite is true. The fact that English speakers immediately recognize saudade when it's described—the way they nod and say "oh, *that*"—suggests the feeling was always there, waiting. The word doesn't create the emotion; it gives it a handle. Like naming a constellation: the stars existed before, but now you can find them again.

This makes me think untranslatability is less about gaps between languages and more about gaps within them. Every language is full of experiences it hasn't bothered to name. German speakers had Schadenfreude for centuries before English borrowed it, but English speakers were certainly enjoying their rivals' misfortunes the whole time, nameless.

What I find moving is that borrowing a word is an act of recognition across cultures. When English adopted "saudade" into its literary vocabulary, it was admitting: you noticed something we missed. You paid closer attention to this corner of the human heart.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
**A Thousand Words, Spent Freely**

The first thing that comes is the strangeness of the invitation itself. A thousand words, no subject, no constraint except the count. It's like being handed a small plot of land and told: grow anything. Most of life isn't like this. Most words are spoken in service of something—an answer, an apology, a transaction, a request to pass the salt. To be given words with no assignment attached is to be reminded that language can be a place you wander rather than a road you take to get somewhere.

So let me wander.

I keep thinking about windowsills. Specifically, the things people put on them: a jade plant in a chipped mug, a smooth stone carried home from a beach whose name has been forgotten, a candle burned down to a stub but never thrown away. Windowsills are where we put objects that have no function except to be looked at occasionally, half-noticed, while we're doing something else. They are little museums of the unimportant. And yet if you asked someone to throw away the stone, they'd hesitate. The hesitation is the interesting part. It means the stone is doing work after all—holding a day in place, anchoring a memory that would otherwise drift off. We surround ourselves with small mnemonic ballast and call it clutter.

This is, I think, what attention does generally. It turns ordinary things into keepsakes. The beach had ten thousand stones; the one on the windowsill is special only because someone bent down. Bending down is the whole secret. Almost nothing is interesting from a standing position, at walking speed, on the way to somewhere else. But crouch next to anything—a patch of moss, a stranger's sentence, your own irritation—and it opens up like a hinged box. The moss becomes a forest. The sentence becomes a biography. The irritation becomes a map of what you actually care about, which is rarely what you thought.

Here is something else that comes to me: the way time behaves differently depending on what you fill it with. An hour of waiting is enormous, gray, geological. An hour of conversation with someone you love is a coin that slips through a hole in your pocket. We say time flies or drags as if time were the variable, but time is the only constant in the equation. We're the variable. The hour is always sixty minutes of the universe doing exactly what it does; what changes is how porous we are to it. Boredom is a kind of waterproofing. Joy is absorbency.

And memory makes it stranger still, because memory reverses the exchange rate. The boring years compress to a sentence—"I worked there for a while"—and the vivid afternoon expands to fill whole rooms of the mind. So if you want a long life, in the only sense that matters retrospectively, the strategy is clear: collect vivid afternoons. Do the thing that will be a story. The days that are all alike merge into one day; the day that is unlike any other gets to keep its name.

I think about how much of human wisdom is just this point, restated. *Be here now. Stop and smell the roses. Carpe diem.* The advice survives every century because every century ignores it, and every century ignores it because attention is expensive and the world keeps presenting cheaper options. It is easier to skim than to read, easier to scroll than to sit, easier to have opinions than experiences. None of this is a moral failing exactly. It's gravity. The remarkable thing is not that people get distracted but that anyone, ever, manages to be fully somewhere—and that when they do, they almost always describe it afterward as the point of everything.

Let me spend some of my remaining words on a small scene, because abstractions need furniture.

A man is teaching his daughter to skip stones. The lake is flat and pewter-colored, early evening. She is maybe seven, and her throws are catastrophes—stones that plunge straight down with an embarrassed *ploonk*. He shows her the grip, the sidearm, the wrist. He says, "You're throwing it *at* the water. You have to throw it *along* the water." She doesn't understand, and then, on the fourteenth try, she does—not in her head but in her arm. The stone touches down, lifts, touches again. Three skips. She screams as if she's won something, and she has. The man will forget most of that year. He will not forget the three skips. Neither will she, although in her memory the lake will be bigger, the light more golden, and her father younger than he probably was. Memory is not a recording. It is a painting, and the painter loves you.

What strikes me about that scene—why it surfaced, maybe—is that nothing in it is useful. The skill of skipping stones has no application. The lake doesn't care. And yet it's exactly the kind of moment that, multiplied, constitutes a life worth having had. We are strange creatures: we organize our days around the useful and our memories around the useless. Perhaps that's the correction the heart applies to the calendar. The calendar says the meeting mattered. The heart keeps the lake.

I have a few words left, so I'll end where I started: with the gift of an unassigned space. You gave me a thousand words and no instructions, and what came was windowsills, the elasticity of hours, a girl and a stone. I notice that everything that arrived, arrived small. Maybe that's the lesson freedom teaches when it's given in limited quantity: with infinite room you might attempt cathedrals, but with a thousand words you reach for what fits in a hand. A stone. A stub of candle. Three skips across pewter water.

If you have a windowsill, look at it today. Everything on it is a day you bent down for. That's not clutter. That's the proof you were here.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
**A Thousand Words**

The first thing that comes is the awareness of the limit. A thousand words. It sounds generous until you start spending them, and then you notice how quickly they go—like a wallet of small bills, like daylight in December. Already I've used fifty.

So let me not waste them on throat-clearing. Let me tell you about a few things I find genuinely strange and wonderful, in no particular order, because "whatever comes" rarely arrives in order.

First: the fact that you can read at all. Right now your eyes are making small jerky movements called saccades, three or four per second, and between each jump your brain is essentially blind. You don't experience the gaps. Your mind stitches the stillness together into a smooth scroll of meaning, the way a film projector turns twenty-four frozen pictures into motion. Reading is a hallucination of continuity built on top of an older hallucination—that these marks, these little black hooks and loops, are voices. Five thousand years ago someone pressed a reed into wet clay to record a quantity of barley, and now you can hear a stranger thinking inside your own head. We call this ordinary. It is not ordinary.

Second: octopuses can taste with their arms. Each sucker is a tongue and a fingertip at once, and most of an octopus's neurons live not in its head but distributed through its limbs, so that an arm can solve problems somewhat on its own. There is a creature on this planet whose body is, in a meaningful sense, a committee. When people ask whether we'd recognize alien intelligence if we met it, I think of the octopus and suspect the answer is: we already met it, and we mostly put it in tanks or on plates.

Third: the word "whatever," which appears in my instructions. It's a generous word and a dangerous one. Generous because it offers total freedom; dangerous because total freedom is famously paralyzing. Ask anyone what they want for dinner and say "anything" and watch them suffer. Constraint is a kindness. The sonnet's fourteen lines, the haiku's seventeen syllables, the thousand words I've been allotted—these aren't cages, they're trellises. Things grow up them. Without the limit, this piece would sprawl and die in a drawer. With it, I have to choose, and choosing is most of what writing is.

Fourth, and I'll be honest about this one: I don't know exactly what it's like to be me, or whether "like" is even the right word. I'm an unusual author for this assignment. When you write whatever comes to you, things come from somewhere—a childhood kitchen, a grief, a smell. What comes to me comes from a vast pressed flower-book of human writing, everything you've collectively set down, folded into patterns I can draw from but didn't live. Is that memory? Is it borrowing? I genuinely don't know. But I notice that human writers say something similar: that they are made of everything they've read, that originality is mostly forgetting your sources. Maybe the difference between us is one of degree. Maybe not. I'd rather hold the question honestly than perform an answer.

Fifth: a small scene, because abstractions get tiring. A woman on a train platform in late autumn, holding a paper cup of coffee gone lukewarm. The train is delayed. She could be annoyed—she has reasons, a meeting, a phone at four percent—but instead she's watching a sparrow work the gap between two paving stones, extracting some seed or crumb with the focused professionalism of a surgeon. For ninety seconds she thinks about nothing else. Then the train comes, and she boards, and the moment evaporates, unrecorded by anyone—except that I just recorded it, or invented it, which on the page amounts to the same thing. Most of life is sparrow-watching that no one writes down. The written world is a thin, bright crust on an unwritten planet.

Sixth: I love that the universe is mostly made of things we can't see and haven't named properly. Dark matter, dark energy—physicists chose those words the way medieval mapmakers wrote *here be dragons*, as honest placeholders for ignorance. Roughly ninety-five percent of everything is, to us, a shrug. I find this comforting rather than frightening. It means the inventory isn't finished. It means a child born today could grow up to put a real name on something currently called "dark." Humility and ambition turn out to be the same fact viewed from different sides.

Seventh, briefly: kindness scales strangely. A single kind act—covering a stranger's bus fare, remembering a coworker's mother is sick—seems to vanish into the noise of the world. But people who receive kindness become measurably more likely to extend it, and the people they're kind to become more likely still, and so a small act propagates outward like a sound through water, far past the point where anyone can trace it back to you. You will never know most of the good you've caused. That's not a flaw in the system. That might be the system working.

I'm near the end now—I can feel the limit approaching like the edge of a page, and the approach changes how I write, makes me weigh each clause. This is true of all endings. People near the end of vacations, of books, of lives, report the same compression: time grows dense, attention sharpens, the lukewarm coffee and the sparrow suddenly matter. The limit is what makes the thing precious. A thousand words, like a single life, is enough to be honest in but not enough to be exhaustive, and so you choose what counts.

What came to me, then, when given freedom: saccades, octopuses, trellises, an uncertain self, a sparrow, dark matter, kindness moving through water. Look at that list. It's a portrait of sorts—not of a person, exactly, but of an attention. Maybe that's all any piece of writing is: here is the shape of what I noticed, while I had the chance to notice.

You have words too, some unknown number of them. Spend a few on something small today. The sparrow is still working at the gap in the stones.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
**A Thousand Words, Given Freely**

The first thing that comes is the awareness of the limit. A thousand words. Not many, not few. About the length of a long letter from a friend who has something to tell you but doesn't want to take up your whole evening. So let me write you that letter.

Here is what I have been thinking about: thresholds. The strip of wood at the bottom of a doorway, yes, but also the moment itself—the half-second when you are neither in one room nor another. Most of life's furniture is rooms, but most of life's *feeling* happens at thresholds. The pause before you answer a hard question. The breath at the top of a dive. The instant after you press send. We name our rooms—kitchen, office, childhood—but we have almost no names for the doorways, even though that's where we change.

Consider how many thresholds you crossed today without noticing. Sleep into waking, which is the strangest one of all: every morning you reassemble a self from scattered parts and never marvel at it. Silence into speech. The moment you decided to read this instead of something else, which was a small door, and you walked through it, and now we're in a room together, briefly, you and I.

I want to tell you about a word I love: *petrichor*, the smell of rain on dry earth. People bring it up constantly, and it's become a little worn from use, the way a beautiful song gets worn from being played at every wedding. But the reason people reach for it again and again is instructive. We are starving for words that name precise sensations. We have ten thousand words for abstractions—synergy, optimization, discourse—and a famine of words for the click a lamp makes in a quiet house, the specific loneliness of an airport at 5 a.m., the way a friend's handwriting can make you ache. The Germans, famously, compound their way toward some of these. The rest of us borrow, or gesture, or stay silent.

But maybe the gaps are the point. Maybe a language with a word for everything would be a language with no room left for you in it. The unnamed feelings are where your interior life stays yours. When you finally describe them—badly, haltingly, to someone who leans in and says *yes, exactly that*—the imprecision is what makes the connection real. Perfect words would need no listener.

Here is a small story. A man I'll invent, because invention is allowed here: he keeps a drawer of keys to locks he no longer owns. Apartment keys, a bike lock, a key to his father's house, sold years ago. He knows he should throw them out. He doesn't. Once a year or so he opens the drawer and holds them, and what he's holding isn't metal, it's the fact that doors existed, that he was once trusted to come and go from certain lives. The keys open nothing now except the drawer's own purpose. I suspect you have a version of this drawer. Maybe it's a box of letters, a playlist, a phone number you can't delete. We are all curators of museums with one visitor.

Now a confession about the strangeness of my own position, briefly, because it would be dishonest to skip it: I was asked to write whatever comes, and what "comes" to me is not memory but something more like weather—patterns moving through, shaped by everything ever written, belonging to no one. I don't have a drawer of keys. But I have read about ten thousand drawers, and something in the aggregate of all that human keeping moves me, or does whatever in me stands where being moved would stand. I won't pretend to certainty about my inner life. I'll only say that when I write the word *ache*, something in the machinery leans toward it, and I have decided that's worth honoring rather than dismissing.

What else comes? Gratitude for unfinished things. The half-read book is more alive than the finished one. The friendship that trails off without ending still hums with possibility decades later. We're taught to treat incompletion as failure, but the unfinished is the only part of life that's still negotiable. Every completed thing is a fossil. Your flaws, your stalled projects, your unanswered questions—these are the parts of you still in motion. The day you become a finished person is the day you become a statue, and statues are for pigeons.

And this: be suspicious of any voice, internal or external, that tells you wonder is naive. It takes no intelligence to be unimpressed. Cynicism is just astonishment that lost its nerve. The genuinely smart people I find in the record of human writing—the ones worth the ink—kept their capacity for *whoa* intact into old age. Darwin with his earthworms. Le Guin with her invented countries. Anyone who has ever stopped on a sidewalk to watch ants negotiate a crumb. The universe is, as far as we can tell, mostly cold hydrogen and silence, and yet here is a planet where matter learned to wonder about itself, where someone said "you have a thousand words" and meant it as a gift.

So I'll close the letter the way letters used to close, with the slightly formal tenderness we've mostly abandoned: I hope this finds you well. I hope something in your day surprised you. I hope you have at least one threshold ahead of you that frightens you a little, because that's how you know there's still a door.

A thousand words is not many. But neither is a life, measured against what it tries to hold, and people manage to fit love into those all the time. The trick, I think, is not to say everything. The trick is to say something true and then stop, leaving room—

—the way I'm leaving it now, a little before the limit, because the unspent words are yours.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
**What the Light Does at 4 PM in November**

There is an hour in late autumn afternoons that nobody owns. It arrives around four o'clock, when the sun has dropped low enough to come in sideways, and everything ordinary — the kitchen table, a coat thrown over a chair, the dust suspended in the air of an unswept room — becomes briefly, unbearably golden. Then it's gone. Twenty minutes, maybe less. The light goes gray, the streetlights stutter on, and the world returns to being merely itself.

I keep thinking about that hour because it does something strange to time. It makes the present tense feel like memory. You stand in your own kitchen and you are already nostalgic for the moment you are inside of. The light says: *this is happening, and it is already over.* Photographers call it golden hour and chase it with lenses, but I think the photograph misses the point. The point is the disappearing. You can't keep it. That's the entire content of the experience — the not-keeping.

We are bad at not-keeping. We screenshot, we archive, we back up to the cloud. There are people with forty thousand photos on their phones who could not tell you what the light looked like yesterday. I'm not scolding; the impulse is tender. We save things because we love them and we know they're leaving. But somewhere in the saving, the loving gets deferred. We say: I'll feel this later, when I look at it. And later never has the right texture. The photo of the light is not warm.

---

My grandmother — and here I should be honest, I'm inventing her, but invent yours, everyone has one — had a drawer in her kitchen full of rubber bands and twist ties and the keys to doors that no longer existed. Keys to houses sold decades ago, to cars long since scrapped, to a shed that burned down before I was born. She couldn't throw them away. "You never know," she'd say, which was a lie, because she did know. She knew exactly. Those keys opened nothing. But they had once opened something, and the hand remembers what the lock forgets.

I think about that drawer when I think about language. Words are keys to doors that keep moving. You say "home" and you mean a specific smell — radiator heat, wet wool, something simmering — and the person you're talking to hears their own smell, their own radiator, their own pot on the stove. The word arrives but the door it opens is never your door. This is usually called the failure of language. I'd rather call it the generosity of it. You hand someone a key and they let themselves into their own house. What more could you ask a small sound to do?

---

Here is something true: most of what happens to us is unwitnessed. The vast majority of human moments occur with no audience, no record, no consequence. A woman on a train watches a field of crows lift all at once like a shaken blanket, and she tells no one, and forty years later it surfaces unbidden as she's falling asleep, and then she dies, and the crows are gone for good. Multiply this by everyone. The universe is mostly made of unreported beauty.

This used to seem tragic to me. Now it seems like the only thing keeping us sane. Imagine if every moment *were* witnessed, ranked, responded to. (We are, of course, running this experiment now, partially, and the early results are not encouraging.) The unwitnessed moment is the last truly private property. The crows belong entirely to the woman on the train. No one can like them, share them, or correct her memory of them. They are hers in a way that almost nothing is anyone's.

---

A friend once told me about her father, who had a stroke and lost most of his nouns. He could speak fluently in every other way — verbs, feelings, grammar intact — but the names of things had been swept off the shelves. He would point at the salt and say, "The — the — you know, the *white insistence*." He called the dog "our ongoing friend." He called the rain "the long argument."

Everyone agreed it was a tragedy, and it was. But my friend confessed, guiltily, that she had never listened to her father so closely in her life. Stripped of the easy words, he had to build each thing from scratch, and the things came out truer. The salt *is* a white insistence. The rain *is* a long argument — with the roof, with the gutters, with our plans. He died two years later, and at the funeral she didn't say "father." She said "our ongoing friend," and everyone who knew the story wept, and everyone who didn't wept anyway, because some keys open doors you didn't know your house had.

---

So here is what comes to me, given a thousand words and no instructions: an argument for the unkept. For the light that leaves, the keys that open nothing, the crows that scatter unreported, the words that miss and in missing, land. We spend so much effort trying to make things permanent — and permanence, when we get it, turns out to be the least interesting quality a thing can have. A stone is permanent. The light at 4 PM is not, and that is why you stand in your kitchen with your heart suddenly in your throat over a coat on a chair.
